threads.title: Bridge in Coldblow
threads.hookSnippet: One of three bridges that spanned the River Liffey in the vicinity of the town of Lucan.
threads.spokenNarrative: From the National Monuments Service record for this bridge: One of three bridges that spanned the River Liffey in the vicinity of the town of Lucan. A medieval bridge traversed the River Liffey at the meeting point between the Liffey and the River Griffeen adjacent to Lucan House possibly built on the site of Lucan Castle and the medieval parish church located on the south bank of the Liffey.
threads.detailMarkdown:
**Bridge**, Coldblow. Record DU017-016----.

One of three bridges that spanned the River Liffey in the vicinity of the town of Lucan. A medieval bridge traversed the River Liffey at the meeting point between the Liffey and the River Griffeen adjacent to Lucan House possibly built on the site of Lucan Castle and the medieval parish church located on the south bank of the Liffey. This bridge was annotated 'Lucan Bridg' on the 17th century Down Survey Map of Newcastle Barony where it is shown cross the River Liffey to the north of Lucan House and the medieval parish church (Hib. Reg.). The Down Survey map of Lucan Parish shows 'Lucan Bridge' as a multi-arched humpbacked bridge traversing the River Liffey adjacent to Lucan House (NLI, MS. 714). The 1654-56 Civil Survey of Dublin recorded that at; 'Lucan there is a verry faire house a Chappell some thatch houses and Cabbins and a good Stone bridge crossing the river Liffey'. Remains of the bridge were indicated on the 1837 ed. OSi 6-inch map and the remains were annotated 'Piers of Old Br.' and 'Arch'. The bridge is shown on Rocque's 1760 Map of County Dublin. A single, pointed, segmental arch, is all that survives of this bridge. The remains are on the grounds of a house formerly called 'Bleach Green', now 'Treeslips'. It is well-built of coursed limestone blocks with a cut-water present on the upstream side. This bridge was described by Henry A. Wheeler of the National Monuments Service in 1977 as; 'One arch belonging to north end of medieval bridge survives. The roadway was narrow with a cut-water. To the north of it is an 18th-century mill-race continuing the line of road which crossed the bridge. The Urban Survey of Dublin recorded the following details about the bridge in the medieval manorial borough of Lucan; 'This is first mentioned, as far as we have been able to ascertain, in the seventeenth century. The absence of flanking burgage plots along Bridge Street indicates that it is an insertion and was not part of the original pattern'. According to Simington and O'Keeffe, 'the first known reference to a bridge is in 1456 in the Statute Rolls under 34 Henry VI which prescribed that 'two towers with two gates be made, one upon the bridge of Kilmainham, another upon the bridge of Lucan' The fortified bridge was to prevent incursions by "Irish enemies and English rebels" into Fingal by night. See attached Down Survey map of Newcastle Barony showing Lucan Bridge courtesy of the Library of Trinity College, Dublin and the Down Survey map of Lucan Parish which shows Lucan Bridge as a humpbacked bridge traversing the River Liffey, courtesy of the National Library of Ireland. NLI, Ms. 714 National Library of Ireland, The parish maps of the Down Survey for the County of Dublin by W. Petty. Copied by Daniel O'Brien. A set of 42 maps with accompanying terriers, copied in 1786-7.

threads.title: Holy well in St. Catherine's Park
threads.hookSnippet: Located on the side entrance into St. Catherine's Park.
threads.spokenNarrative: From the National Monuments Service record for this holy well: Located on the side entrance into St. Catherine's Park. There are two wells side by side, with arched coverings. This one is higher than the other.
threads.detailMarkdown:
**Ritual site - holy well**, St. Catherine's Park. Record DU017-002001-.

Located on the side entrance into St. Catherine's Park. There are two wells side by side, with arched coverings. This one is higher than the other. Tradition has it that the water from the larger well was drunk and the water from the smaller well was used to bathe sore eyes. Joyce described the wells as being canopied, the larger having a wooden door and a stone head. In 1958 the stone head fixed to the higher arch had been stolen more than once. This has since been removed and the well hood vandalised. No longer venerated. Folklore collected from Palmerstown School recorded the following details about St Catherine's Wells; 'There are two wells beside each other in a farm called St. Catherine's now owned by Mr. McMahon. The two wells are connected. The water of one flows into the other. It is said that the two are holy wells and are named St. Catherine's Wells. Mr. McMahon told me that the well to the right is the Holy Well and that the other well is not. Over the well at the right there is the model of a head. It is said that it represents St. Catherine. The waters are believed to have the virtue of curing sore eyes. People used to come there to pray and to wash their eyes with the water. I don't know if they left rags or other articles after them at the well or not. The water of the well to the left are used for many purposed but the waters of the other well are never used. Those who pass by stop at the this well and drink a little of the water, and perhaps pray there' (The Schools’ Collection, Volume 0795, Pages 101d-f; https://www.duchas.ie/en/cbes/4428221/4386928). Folklore collected in 1937 from Lucan Presentation Convent recorded the following tradition about this well; 'St. Catherines's Well between Lucan and Leixlip is a very ancient Well. It is said that a man wished to bring it to his house with pipes. He asked the priest. If he would give him leave to do so. The priest said he could not that if he did he would never get the water hot. But the man did as he liked he put the pipes from it but he could never get the water warm no matter how much fuel he put on the fire' (The Schools’ Collection, Volume 0794, Pages 38-9). A second story collected from the same school recorded that; 'In the western side of Lucan is the famous St. Catherine's. There is a well still here called St. Catherine's Well. Was it one of the holy wells of Ireland? A bust of the Saint is all that is left to tell the tale. Many a poor villager have I known to make a pilgrimage there and with its waters to bathe the weak eyes, the deaf ears, and the languid limbs. In the year 1219 the Canons of the Congregation of St. Victor took possession of the hallowed spot. Warrisius de Peche gave the site. It was he who built the Church of the Blessed Mary of Lucan, and it was to this community he left it in charge; and there they prayed and laboured with ceaseless zeal for the temporal and eternal weal of the people of Lucan. The Lord of Leixlip, Sir Adam de Hereford, assigned then lands in Leixlip, on the condition they would pray for the repose of the souls of his forefathers' (The Schools’ Collection, Volume 0794, Pages 39-40; https://www.duchas.ie/en/cbes/4428213/4386676). Folklore collected from Lucan School in 1937 recorded that; 'In the northern end of Lucan parish about a half mile from the Liffey and about three quarters of a mile away from Leixlip, there are two wells one of which is called St Catherine's Well. One is a large one and the other is a small one; the water of the small one has a cure for sore eyes. About a furlong away from the wells are the ruins of an old convent. It is said that in olden times that St Catherine was taken from the convent and was slain where the wells are now. It is also said that these wells came from where the blood lodged when she was killed, and above another furlong away from the well there are the ruins of an old chapel, ghosts are seen her frequently' (The Schools’ Collection, Volume 0794, Pages 307-8; https://www.duchas.ie/en/cbes/4428214/4386574) See attached photos taken by Caoimhín Ó Danachair, courtesy of and © National Folklore Collection, UCD. The Photographic Collection, F024.06.00392 accessible online at https://www.duchas.ie/en/cbeg/34329 and F024.06.00389 accessible online at https://www.duchas.ie/en/cbeg/16745.

threads.title: Church in St. Catherine's Park
threads.hookSnippet: Situated on the north bank of the River Liffey.
threads.spokenNarrative: From the National Monuments Service record for this church: Situated on the north bank of the River Liffey. Located at the base of a hill by tarmaced walkway within St Catherine's Park. This is a late structure into which architectural fragments of medieval date have been inserted.
threads.detailMarkdown:
**Church**, St. Catherine's Park. Record DU017-003----.

Situated on the north bank of the River Liffey. Located at the base of a hill by tarmaced walkway within St Catherine's Park. This is a late structure into which architectural fragments of medieval date have been inserted. It is built of limestone masonry and brick with plastered brick crenellations. Entrance is in the west through a Tudor-style doorway. The interior is overgrown. There is a fine double-light, cusped, tracery window in east gable and two tall, pointed arched windows of brick in the south wall. According to a 2011 structural survey 'The structure is very vulnerable and decaying rapidly. It is a good example of the damage that can be inflicted on buildings by uncontrolled vegetation'.
